triage.name: Crohn's Disease
triage.reason: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease with abdominal pain, diarrhea and weight loss; diagnosis reached by history, exam, labs, imaging and endoscopy.

age.peak: bimodal: late teens to 20s and a second smaller peak in the 50s to 60s

demographics: Slightly more common in females in some series, but overall affects both sexes similarly
More common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry
More common in developed countries and in urban areas
More common in White populations, though it occurs in all races and ethnicities

risk_factors.text: Family history of inflammatory bowel disease in a first-degree relative
Use of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or aspirin

family_history: Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis in a parent, sibling, or child
Other autoimmune disease in the family
social_history: Stress and certain foods may worsen symptoms but do not cause the disease

chief_complaints.text: I've been losing weight without trying
I have pain around my bottom

hpi.onset: Gradual, with intermittent symptoms that come and go over weeks to months
hpi.duration: Often present for weeks to months before diagnosis; may have had milder episodes for longer
hpi.progression: Symptoms wax and wane in flares; diarrhea and cramping become more frequent and weight loss accumulates over time
hpi.location: Diffuse or lower abdominal cramping, often right lower quadrant or periumbilical
hpi.radiation: Usually none; pain may be referred to the back with severe inflammation
hpi.quality: Crampy, colicky abdominal pain; diarrhea is often loose to watery and may be urgent
hpi.severity: Moderate; pain 4–7/10 during flares, milder between flares
hpi.timing: Pain often comes in waves before a bowel movement and eases afterward; diarrhea may wake the patient at night
aggravating: Eating, especially high-fiber or fatty foods

associated_symptoms.text: Red, tender bumps under the skin, often on the shins

pertinent_negatives: Bloody diarrhea as the main symptom
Tenesmus (constant feeling of needing to pass stool)
Recent travel or sick contacts with similar diarrhea
Nocturnal diarrhea is present in Crohn's but bloody stools are less typical than in ulcerative colitis

positives.text: Urgency to have a bowel movement

negatives: Bloody stools as the predominant symptom
Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Back pain that wakes the patient at night
argues_against: Ankylosing spondylitis as the sole diagnosis

positives.text: Red, tender bumps on the shins

negatives: Rash after starting a new medication

positives.text: Pallor or easy fatigue from anemia

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with growth failure, delayed puberty, and poor weight gain rather than prominent diarrhea or pain.
Presentation may be milder or mistaken for diverticular disease or ischemic colitis; a second peak occurs in the 50s to 60s.
Symptoms may flare or remit; active disease increases risk of preterm birth and low birth weight, and some medications need adjustment.
Infectious colitis and medication-related colitis are more likely and must be excluded before attributing symptoms to Crohn's.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable at rest, no distress; may look tired
general.moderate: Mildly ill-appearing, thin, uncomfortable during the interview, shifting in the chair
general.severe: Ill-appearing, visibly thin or wasted, pale, diaphoretic, guarding the abdomen
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, cachectic, pale, hypotensive and tachycardic, lethargic or confused

Distension with tympany, suggesting obstruction or ileus

Palpate the cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph node chains

labs.caveat: A normal CRP does not exclude Crohn's disease; it is more often normal in isolated ileal disease.
Anemia of chronic disease plus iron deficiency from chronic blood loss; may be normocytic or microcytic.
Reactive thrombocytosis from chronic inflammation; a low platelet count should raise concern for another process.
A normal or only mildly elevated white count is common; marked leukocytosis suggests abscess or another infection.
Low albumin reflects inflammation, poor intake and protein-losing enteropathy; a low level marks more severe disease.
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may look normal despite iron deficiency when inflammation is active.
Low when the terminal ileum is involved or has been resected.
Low with fat malabsorption and vitamin D deficiency; check the corrected calcium when albumin is low.
A very high CRP with fever and focal tenderness should prompt imaging for abscess.
Not routinely needed; a high value favors bacterial infection or abscess over a Crohn's flare.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and before starting immunosuppressive therapy.

Not routinely needed; consider only if diarrhea persists without inflammation

Pregnancy test before CT or immunosuppressive therapy in anyone who could be pregnant
Use MRI instead of CT in children and pregnancy to avoid radiation

Fever with focal tenderness or a mass should prompt imaging for abscess before any surgery

criteria.name: Diagnosis of Crohn's disease
criteria.summary: A compatible chronic relapsing history plus objective evidence of segmental, transmural inflammation on endoscopy, histology or cross-sectional imaging, after excluding infection and other causes of colitis.
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss or growth failure
Endoscopic patchy inflammation with skip lesions and rectal sparing
Biopsy showing transmural inflammation, crypt distortion or noncaseating granulomas
Cross-sectional imaging showing bowel wall thickening, stricture, fistula or abscess

differential.name: Ulcerative Colitis
differential.why_considered: The other major inflammatory bowel disease; chronic diarrhea and abdominal cramping in a young adult
differential.trigger: Bloody diarrhea with tenesmus and urgency

history: Bloody diarrhea as the predominant symptom
Tenesmus and small-volume, frequent stools
Continuous symptoms rather than discrete flares with normal intervals
No perianal pain or drainage
exam: No perianal fistula, fissure or abscess
Tenderness along the colon rather than right lower quadrant
labs: Positive p-ANCA more often than ASCA
Fecal calprotectin elevated in both, so it does not separate them
imaging: Continuous inflammation starting at the rectum and extending proximally without skip lesions
No terminal ileum involvement (backwash ileitis only with severe pancolitis)
Lead pipe colon with loss of haustra in chronic disease

differential.name: Intestinal Tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Granulomatous ileocecal inflammation that mimics Crohn's on biopsy and imaging
differential.trigger: Granulomas on biopsy with fever, night sweats, weight loss, or a history of travel or residence in a high-prevalence area

history: Fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss
Travel to or residence in a country with high tuberculosis prevalence
Known tuberculosis exposure or prior pulmonary disease
No chronic relapsing diarrhea pattern
exam: Right lower quadrant mass or tenderness
labs: Positive interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test
Acid-fast bacilli or caseating granulomas on biopsy
Positive mycobacterial culture or PCR from tissue
imaging: Caseating granulomas rather than noncaseating granulomas
Circumferential ileocecal thickening with enlarged necrotic lymph nodes
Chest radiograph showing active or prior pulmonary tuberculosis

differential.name: Infectious Colitis
differential.why_considered: Acute diarrhea, cramping and fever can look like a Crohn's flare
differential.trigger: Acute onset over days, sick contacts, recent travel, or antibiotic exposure

history: Acute onset over hours to days rather than weeks to months
Sick contacts with similar diarrhea or a common food exposure
Recent antibiotic use suggesting C. difficile
Recent travel to an area with endemic infection
exam: Diffuse abdominal tenderness without a right lower quadrant mass
Signs of dehydration rather than chronic weight loss
labs: Positive stool culture, C. difficile toxin/PCR, or ova and parasites
Fecal calprotectin may be elevated, so it does not exclude infection
imaging: Diffuse colonic inflammation without skip lesions or terminal ileum thickening
No stricture, fistula or creeping fat

differential.name: Celiac Disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, weight loss and fatigue in a young adult

history: Diarrhea and bloating triggered by gluten-containing foods
Symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet
No perianal disease or mouth ulcers
Family history of celiac disease
exam: Signs of malabsorption such as dermatitis herpetiformis or glossitis
No abdominal mass or perianal findings
labs: Positive tissue transglutaminase IgA with elevated total IgA
Iron deficiency anemia and low folate
imaging: Small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia
No skip lesions, stricture or fistula on cross-sectional imaging

differential.name: Irritable Bowel Syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits in a young adult

history: Pain relieved by defecation and associated with a change in stool frequency or form
No weight loss, fever, or nocturnal diarrhea
Symptoms fluctuate with stress rather than following a progressive inflammatory course
No family history of inflammatory bowel disease
exam: Normal abdominal exam without tenderness, mass or perianal findings
No signs of malnutrition or anemia
labs: Normal CRP, ESR, hemoglobin and albumin
imaging: No bowel wall thickening, skip lesions or stricture

differential.name: Behçet Disease
differential.why_considered: Mouth and intestinal ulcers with abdominal pain can mimic Crohn's

history: Recurrent painful oral and genital ulcers
Eye inflammation with redness and photophobia
Skin lesions such as acneiform nodules or a positive pathergy response
No chronic diarrhea as the dominant symptom
exam: Pathergy reaction at a needle puncture site
labs: No specific serologic test; diagnosis is clinical
Inflammatory markers may be elevated during flares
imaging: Ileocecal ulcers that are deep and round rather than serpiginous
No creeping fat or noncaseating granulomas on biopsy

differential.name: Diverticulitis
differential.why_considered: Left lower quadrant pain, fever and leukocytosis in an older adult

history: Acute onset over hours to days rather than a chronic relapsing course
Pain localized to the left lower quadrant
Constipation more common than chronic diarrhea
No weight loss or extraintestinal manifestations
exam: Left lower quadrant tenderness with guarding
No perianal fistula or oral ulcers
labs: Normal hemoglobin and albumin in uncomplicated cases
imaging: Colonic diverticula with segmental wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding
No terminal ileum involvement or skip lesions

differential.name: Ischemic Colitis
differential.why_considered: Abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea in an older adult with vascular risk factors

history: Sudden onset of crampy pain followed by urgency to defecate
Older age with atrial fibrillation, heart failure or vascular disease
Symptoms often resolve over days to weeks
No chronic waxing and waning pattern
exam: Mild abdominal tenderness without a mass
No perianal disease or extraintestinal findings
labs: Leukocytosis and anemia from acute blood loss
imaging: Segmental colonic wall thickening, often in a watershed distribution such as the splenic flexure
No terminal ileum involvement or creeping fat

severity.mild: Ambulatory, fewer than 4 loose stools per day, minimal cramping, no fever, no weight loss, normal or near-normal inflammatory markers and albumin; no anemia or dehydration
severity.moderate: 4 to 6 loose stools per day, intermittent cramping, low-grade fever, some weight loss, mildly elevated CRP or ESR, mild anemia, no obstruction or abscess
severity.severe: More than 6 loose stools per day, persistent pain, fever, significant weight loss, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, elevated inflammatory markers, or imaging showing stricture, fistula or phlegmon
severity.critical: Toxic presentation with high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, severe abdominal tenderness or distension, marked leukocytosis, and imaging showing abscess, perforation or bowel obstruction requiring urgent intervention

red_flags.finding: High fever with focal abdominal tenderness or a palpable mass
red_flags.meaning: Suggests intra-abdominal abscess or phlegmon; needs urgent imaging and possible drainage

red_flags.finding: Diffuse abdominal rigidity or rebound tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests perforation with peritonitis; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Vomiting, abdominal distension and absent or high-pitched bowel sounds
red_flags.meaning: Suggests bowel obstruction from stricture or adhesions; needs urgent imaging and surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Tachycardia, hypotension or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Suggests sepsis or hypovolemia from severe inflammation or blood loss; resuscitate and investigate urgently

red_flags.finding: Grossly bloody stools with hemodynamic instability
red_flags.meaning: Suggests severe lower gastrointestinal bleeding; needs urgent resuscitation and endoscopy

red_flags.finding: Severe perianal pain with fluctuance or drainage
red_flags.meaning: Suggests perianal or ischiorectal abscess; needs urgent surgical drainage

complications.name: Intestinal stricture with obstruction
clues: Progressive cramping and distension after meals
Vomiting and inability to pass stool or gas
Dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels on abdominal x-ray

complications.name: Fistula formation
clues: Drainage of stool or pus from the perianal skin, vagina or abdominal wall
Recurrent urinary tract infections or pneumaturia from an enterovesical fistula
Fistula tract on pelvic MRI or CT enterography

complications.name: Intra-abdominal or perianal abscess
clues: High fever with focal tenderness or a palpable mass
Marked leukocytosis and very high CRP
Rim-enhancing fluid collection on CT or MRI

complications.name: Perforation with peritonitis
clues: Sudden severe abdominal pain with rigidity
Free air under the diaphragm on upright chest or abdominal x-ray
Hypotension and tachycardia

complications.name: Severe lower gastrointestinal bleeding
clues: Large-volume bloody stools
Falling hemoglobin and hemodynamic instability
Active bleeding on colonoscopy

complications.name: Malnutrition and micronutrient deficiency
clues: Weight loss and muscle wasting
Low albumin, iron, vitamin B12, folate, calcium or vitamin D
Growth failure in children

complications.name: Venous thromboembolism
clues: Unilateral leg swelling and pain
Sudden dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain
Risk is highest during active flares and hospitalization

complications.name: Colorectal cancer
clues: Long-standing colonic disease, especially more than 8 to 10 years
New anemia, rectal bleeding or change in bowel habit
Dysplasia or mass on surveillance colonoscopy

special_populations.differences: Growth failure, delayed puberty and poor weight gain may be the presenting features rather than prominent diarrhea or pain; upper GI involvement is more common and MRI is preferred to avoid radiation.
A second peak occurs in the 50s to 60s; presentation may be milder or mistaken for diverticular or ischemic colitis, and complications such as stricture and cancer are more common.
Active disease increases the risk of preterm birth and low birth weight; some medications need adjustment, and MRI without gadolinium is preferred for imaging when possible.

Infectious colitis and medication-related colitis are more likely and must be excluded before attributing symptoms to a Crohn's flare; immunosuppressive therapy increases the risk of serious infections.

key_questions.question: How long have you had diarrhea, and how many loose stools a day?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic diarrhea lasting weeks to months, often 4 or more loose stools per day during flares

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and what is it like?
key_questions.looking_for: Crampy, colicky pain, often right lower quadrant or periumbilical, coming in waves before a bowel movement

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss, often 5-10% or more, supporting chronic inflammatory disease

key_questions.question: Do your symptoms come and go, or are they continuous?
key_questions.looking_for: Waxing and waning flares with relatively normal intervals, typical of Crohn's

key_questions.question: Does the diarrhea wake you at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal diarrhea, which favors organic inflammatory disease over irritable bowel syndrome

key_questions.question: Is there blood or mucus in your stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Blood less prominent than in ulcerative colitis; mucus may be present

key_questions.question: Do you have pain, itching, or drainage around your bottom?
key_questions.looking_for: Perianal pain, fissure, fistula drainage, or abscess, which strongly supports Crohn's

key_questions.question: Have you had mouth sores, joint pain, eye redness, or skin bumps?
key_questions.looking_for: Extraintestinal manifestations such as aphthous ulcers, arthritis, uveitis, or erythema nodosum

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade fever in flares; high fever with chills suggests abscess or infection

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or another autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of inflammatory bowel disease in a first-degree relative

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or have you ever smoked?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or past smoking, a strong risk factor for Crohn's

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including NSAIDs, birth control pills, or antibiotics?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, or recent antibiotics, which may increase risk or worsen symptoms

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently or been around anyone with similar diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Travel or sick contacts that would suggest infectious colitis instead

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status, which affects imaging and treatment choices

key_questions.question: Have you had any abdominal surgery or bowel resections?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior surgery for Crohn's complications or other abdominal conditions

reasoning_points: Chronic diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and unintentional weight loss over weeks to months
Waxing and waning course with flares and relatively normal intervals
Right lower quadrant or periumbilical tenderness on exam
Perianal findings such as fissure, fistula, or abscess supporting Crohn's over ulcerative colitis
Extraintestinal manifestations such as aphthous ulcers, arthritis, uveitis, or erythema nodosum
Elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) and anemia of chronic disease or iron deficiency
Fecal calprotectin elevated, distinguishing inflammatory diarrhea from irritable bowel syndrome
Stool studies negative for infection, including C. difficile, before attributing symptoms to Crohn's
Colonoscopy showing patchy, discontinuous inflammation with skip lesions, rectal sparing, and terminal ileum involvement
Biopsy showing transmural inflammation, crypt architectural distortion, or noncaseating granulomas
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MR enterography) showing bowel wall thickening, stricture, fistula, or abscess
Pregnancy test negative before imaging and immunosuppressive therapy when applicable

easy: Young adult with months of diarrhea, crampy right lower quadrant pain, and weight loss
Perianal fistula or fissure found on exam
Elevated CRP and ESR with anemia
Colonoscopy with classic skip lesions and cobblestoning
medium: Symptoms overlap with ulcerative colitis; bloody diarrhea is minimal or absent
Predominantly ileal disease with normal colonoscopy unless terminal ileum is intubated
Extraintestinal manifestations such as joint pain or eye redness dominate the presentation
Older adult with a second peak of incidence, symptoms mistaken for diverticulitis
Normal CRP despite active isolated ileal disease
hard: Child with growth failure and delayed puberty but minimal GI symptoms
Pregnant patient with abdominal pain and diarrhea; imaging and treatment must be adjusted
Immunocompromised patient where infectious colitis must be excluded first
Presentation with a complication such as stricture, fistula, or abscess rather than classic symptoms
Granulomas on biopsy raising intestinal tuberculosis as a mimic in a patient with relevant travel history
